lessons.title: Overview, Context & Style
lessons.description: Rise Up by Lisa Evans — the Freedom Riders, abstract style, cast, conventions, and how to open a Section B essay.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction to Rise Up

For Section B of your OCR Drama exam, you must write about a live theatre performance you have seen. You need to analyse and evaluate the acting, design elements, and how meaning was communicated to the audience.

The performance you watched was ‘Rise Up’ by Lisa Evans for the Theatre Centre, performed at Unity College’s Auditorium. Section B is an essay question worth 30 marks — 20 marks for answering the question and 10 marks for using drama terminology. You have 30 minutes to write your response.

Key Fact — Section B Requirements

Every Section B answer must state the name of the play, where you watched it, and when. You will be asked to either analyse or evaluate an aspect of the performance. Always include: a clear example of what you observed, why it was effective, its impact on you and the audience, and how it could be developed.

Key Fact — Paragraph Structure for Section B

Every paragraph in your Section B answer must follow this structure:

  • Thumbs up (Positive): Give an example of something that was successful and justify why it was effective.
  • Thumb towards yourself (Impact): Explain the impact on you or the audience — what did it make you think, feel, or understand?
  • Thumbs down (Development): Suggest a development and justify why that change would be even more effective.

Remember: every paragraph needs all three — positive, impact, and development.

Synopsis: The Freedom Riders

‘Rise Up’ is a play within a play. A group of four British actors meet to discuss and educate the audience about the Freedom Riders of 1960s America. The play explores how a group of Black and White protesters set off on an epic journey from Washington to the Southern States of America to expose racism.

Despite laws making segregation illegal, Black people were still not welcome in White establishments and were not allowed to sit where they wished on buses and coaches. The Freedom Riders wanted to show that this discrimination was still happening. They encountered violent racist protests in which some lost their lives and were often arrested or dumped in Ku Klux Klan territories by the police — despite having the backing of the American government.

The play explores several important themes:

  • Equality and Racism — the central focus, demonstrated by the Freedom Riders’ journey and the violent opposition they faced
  • Relationships — shown through the bonds between the Freedom Riders, and between the Little White Girl and her racist family
  • Violence — demonstrated by the attack on the Freedom Riders’ bus in Birmingham, Alabama
  • Ambitions — shown through Diane Nash’s determination to achieve equality through non-violent protest

Style: Abstract with Naturalism

The playwright states at the start: “Form: Fluid storytelling in which actors can move from character to character with precise and efficient movement. The piece should be played with truth but not naturalistically.”

The style of the play was abstract, with moments of naturalism. This allowed the audience to see how the characters felt and interacted with each other. The abstract style meant performers faced out towards the audience and used symbolic staging rather than realistic settings.

Key Fact — Genre

Rise Up is documentary drama. All the information is based on documented evidence and facts about the real Freedom Riders, though some names were changed to protect characters. It is also educational and informative, designed to teach the audience about what actually happened in 1960s America. The meaning of the play is to encourage audiences to solve problems without violence and to question their own opinions and beliefs.

The Cast

Rise Up was performed by just four actors who used multi-rolling to portray many different characters throughout the performance:

  • Em (Emma Dennis-Edwards) — a Black female performer who played multiple roles including a Freedom Rider in the bus explosion and an old Black lady offering refuge
  • CJ (Sam Kacher) — the only White performer, who played Governor Patterson, Bobby Kennedy, and the Little White Girl
  • Dayz (Kimisha Lewis) — a Black female performer who played Diane Nash and a Freedom Rider on the bus
  • Ty (Edward Nkom) — a Black male performer who played Uncle George, Jim, and a young Freedom Rider

The performance used several drama conventions that you should reference in your exam:

  • Narration — actors stepped out of character to narrate events directly to the audience, helping them understand the context
  • Flashback — used to show historical events such as Diane Nash addressing students at Fisk University
  • Sound collage — multiple voices speaking simultaneously to build tension and create a climax
  • Ensemble movement — actors moving in synchronisation to show unity or to mark key moments
  • Choral work — actors speaking in unison to show shared opinions (e.g. the White shoppers)
  • Facing out — all performers face the audience, reinforcing the abstract style
  • Marking the moment — slow motion used during the bus explosion to emphasise its significance

Writing Your Opening Paragraph

Every Section B response must begin with a summarising paragraph. This puts the play into context for the reader and shows your understanding. Here is an example:

“I watched the play ‘Rise Up’ by Lisa Evans for the Theatre Centre, at Unity College’s Auditorium. The play explores the fight against racism in America in the 1960s. A group of Blacks and Whites, the Freedom Riders, set off on an epic journey from Washington to the Southern States of America to expose racism. They wanted to show, despite laws making segregation illegal, that Blacks were still not welcome in White establishments and were not allowed to sit where they wished on buses and coaches.”

The SEAS Paragraph Structure

Every paragraph in your Section B essay should follow the SEAS structure:

  • S — State what you observed (a clear example from the performance)
  • E — Explain why it was effective, using drama terminology
  • A — Audience — discuss the impact on you and the audience
  • S — Suggest a development — how could it have been improved and why?
Key Fact — Useful Evaluation Phrases

Build these phrases into your writing: “This was effective because…”, “In my opinion I thought…”, “However, in reflection…”, “I particularly enjoyed…”, and “I feel that this could have been developed because…”
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Section B, you are not being asked to tell the story. A good answer shows that you analyse and evaluate specific performance and design choices. Always use the SEAS paragraph structure: State what you saw, Explain why it was effective using drama terminology, describe the Audience impact, and Suggest a development. Remember — 10 of the 30 marks are specifically for using drama terminology, so make every sentence count.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ‘Rise Up’ by Lisa Evans is a documentary drama performed in an abstract style with moments of naturalism, telling the story of the Freedom Riders in 1960s America.
  • Four actors use multi-rolling to play many characters, with conventions including narration, flashback, sound collage, and ensemble movement.
  • Your Section B essay must state where and when you watched the play, follow the SEAS paragraph structure, and use drama terminology throughout — 10 of the 30 marks are for terminology alone.

lessons.title: Key Moments — White Shoppers & Bus Explosion
lessons.description: Analysing voice, physicality, and staging in the White Shoppers and Bus Explosion scenes.
lessons.content_html:
Key Moment One: White Shoppers Scene

The White Shoppers scene takes place at Forsythe & Sons grocery store (timestamp 13:50 in the recorded version). It begins with the line “Next stop, Anniston, Alabama.” This scene introduces the Little White Girl (LWG) and reveals the casual, everyday racism that the Freedom Riders were fighting against.

Positioning and Staging

The LWG (a 12-year-old character) sat on a tall stool centre stage. The White shoppers were positioned upstage right (USR) while they put on their white gloves, then took a step in — reducing proxemics — on the name of the store to highlight the location to the audience. The LWG’s mum was positioned upstage left (USL).

Three steel flats at the back of the space represented the Greyhound bus the Freedom Riders were travelling on. Only the tall stool centre stage was used in this scene, with small stools positioned stage left and stage right, and a tall stool at the back of the space USR.

Key Fact — Why Positioning Matters

The LWG being placed on the tall stool centre stage made her the focal point of the scene. This positioning highlighted her innocence and the significance of her questioning of racism. The White shoppers staying USL showed they were a united group, separate from the LWG, reinforcing that racist attitudes were normalised in this community.

Voice Techniques in the White Shoppers Scene

The White female shoppers spoke in a high pitch and in unison: “we do, we do.” This suggested their opinions were identical. The high pitch suggested to the audience that they were “air heads” who did not think for themselves.

The LWG’s mum said “the coloured folk can do their shopping down their part of town” — here “their” was emphasised by elongating the word. This drew the audience’s attention to the discrimination the Freedom Riders were fighting against.

When the LWG questioned “why?” she used a higher pitch at the end of the word to show she was genuinely questioning her mum. This demonstrated to the audience that the child could not see any reason why people should be treated differently because of their colour.

The mum replied “just different honey, that’s all you need to know” using a high pitch, which suggested she had no real justification for her answer and highlighted her lack of education on the subject. The shoppers then spoke “We’re happy” in unison, again using a very high-pitched voice to reinforce they were not thinking independently.

Physicality in the White Shoppers Scene

The White female shoppers stood in very close proximity of one another, linking their arms as if they were one person. They aggressively fanned the hand covered in the white glove — a quick-paced movement that was echoed by the LWG’s mum. The LWG’s mum emphasised “their” further with a double flick of the wrist in a derogatory fashion, as if dismissing someone, suggesting she felt that Black people were beneath her.

When the LWG said “why?”, all attention was placed on her. Em and Dayz immediately stopped fanning and made direct eye contact with the LWG. The mum moved her head sharply to stare at the LWG — this physicality showed the performers were shocked at the question, because it was not in line with their racist thinking.

Key Fact — Costume Detail

The only addition to the base costumes in this scene was a single white glove for each female performer playing a White shopper. Dayz put on the left-hand glove and Em put on the right-hand glove — reinforcing that they “are as one” and that their racist thinking was aligned. Ty had no costume change but used physicality changes (holding hands pinched together at waist height) to create his character.

A white and blue lighting wash was used at the start of the scene. The blue tinge was emphasised by the reflection of the steel flats, suggesting loneliness and isolation for the Freedom Riders. When the line “Such a beautiful day” was spoken, the white light intensity increased and the blue was removed, symbolising the sun through the bus window.

When the LWG was introduced, the white lighting wash increased in intensity and the blue colour was removed entirely. This bright white lighting symbolised the innocence of the LWG and her purity.

Key Moment Two: The Bus Explosion Scene

The bus explosion scene (timestamp 15:54) begins with Uncle George shouting “Hey, Hey!” This scene depicts the violent attack on the Freedom Riders’ bus when it arrived in Birmingham, Alabama. It is one of the most powerful moments in the performance, building to an intense climax.

Positioning and Levels in the Bus Explosion

Centre stage left, a small stool and a tall stool were placed directly next to one another in close proxemics. Uncle George (played by Ty) stood with one leg on the tall stool and one on the small stool, widening his gait to make the character seem larger, more imposing, and more intimidating. His position on the highest level signified his power as the ringleader of the White mob.

USR, CJ sat on the tall stool looking directly at Uncle George. Em stood in front of a small stool almost centre of stage right, watching the actor in role as Uncle George. Dayz stood downstage left with her back to the audience. All actors having direct eye contact on Uncle George showed he was the most significant character in this moment.

On the line “Hey, stop, stop ’em, that bus with Yankees, Jews and uppity blacks sitting in the wrong place,” Uncle George outstretched his right arm using strong muscle tension and a pointing gesture, directing the audience’s attention to the bus and showing his anger was aimed at everyone on board. He used an aggressive tone, quick pace, and loud volume.

On “We’ll show them their place,” UG stepped onto the highest stool and tensed both fists at his sides in an intimidating fashion. Contrastingly, this line was spoken in a quieter volume with a calm tone, as if UG had the right to decide who could visit his hometown — highlighting his ignorance and lack of empathy.

On “No darks and Yankee’s are going to tell us how to behave,” he used a quick-paced pointing gesture at himself with his thumb while his hand remained in a fist — the fist “threatened” the Freedom Riders. The emphasis on “us” was created by a short pause before and after the word.

The Freedom Riders on the Bus

When Dayz and Em took on the roles of Freedom Riders, they each took a small stool and placed them in close proximity centre stage, gripping the sides with very strong muscle tension as if holding on to the edge of their seats on the bus. This simple physicality helped the audience imagine the bus clearly, creating empathy.

Dayz used quick-paced breaths and exaggerated shoulder movements to show fear, with fidgety movements as she looked around for comfort. In contrast, Em’s Freedom Rider was much more static and composed, sitting facing forward and making direct eye contact with the audience whilst reciting the Lord’s Prayer. This contrast in physicality effectively highlighted the panic of the situation and how different people react differently when faced with the same danger.

Key Fact — Ensemble Movement and Slow Motion

During the explosion, Em and Dayz moved their arms up to protect their heads in slow motion. This was effective because it marked the most serious moment and symbolised that the Freedom Riders were not violent — their movement was a passive protest. Using slow motion rather than having the characters fall to the floor suggested they had not lost any power by remaining non-violent.

Lighting: When UG said “Throw it in” and “burn ’em, burn ’em alive,” a small orange shaft of light appeared USC on the middle steel flat, showing the audience the bus was now alight. The intensity increased gradually until “the engine’s going to blow” when the orange reached its peak. The white wash faded to a much lower intensity, making the orange flames stand out. The orange light created shadows on the flats, creating the illusion of a crowd of Freedom Riders — making the audience feel there were many people in danger.

Sound: A banging sound effect was used as if someone was banging on the side of the bus, emphasised by the Freedom Riders asking “What’s that noise?” Faint sounds of a crowd talking and small bangs built gradually. A small explosion sound was used when UG said “the engine’s going to blow.” A sound collage built the climax: Em repeated the Lord’s Prayer, UG shouted “burn, negro lovers, burn,” the LWG narrated, and Dayz panicked saying “they’re going to burn us alive.”
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about key moments, always describe the specific performance skills you observed — don’t just say “the actor was good.” Name the technique (tone, pace, pitch, volume, muscle tension, proxemics, levels, gesture) and explain what it communicated to the audience. For example: “The White shoppers spoke in unison using a high pitch, which suggested they did not think for themselves and highlighted the conformity of racist attitudes in the Southern States.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The White Shoppers scene uses unison speech, white gloves, and direct eye contact to show conformity and the normalisation of racist attitudes in 1960s America.
  • The Bus Explosion scene builds to a powerful climax using levels, muscle tension, lighting changes (orange for fire), sound collage, and contrasting physicality between the Freedom Riders.
  • The slow-motion ensemble movement during the explosion marked the moment and symbolised the Freedom Riders’ non-violent protest — a powerful staging choice to analyse in your exam.

lessons.title: Key Moments — Diane Nash & CJ Reminder
lessons.description: Analysing voice, physicality, and staging in the Diane Nash phone call and CJ Reminder scenes.
lessons.content_html:
Key Moment Three: Diane Nash Phone Conversation

This scene occurs at approximately 27 minutes into the performance. It begins when Bobby Kennedy, the Attorney General, asks “Who the hell is Diane Nash?” Diane Nash was a real-life student activist at Fisk University in Nashville who organised a second wave of Freedom Riders after the first group were attacked.

Staging and Positioning

The scene had two distinct staging arrangements. In the flashback to the university, Diane Nash (Dayz) was positioned centre stage with CJ, Em, and Ty sat on the floor in a circle surrounding her. They each pulled their knees to their chests and made direct eye contact with Diane Nash, straining their necks to see her. This effectively highlighted that the students were interested in the cause and listening intently.

Diane Nash’s higher level in this moment reminded the audience she was in control and taking charge of the situation. The other actors sitting at a lower level showed she held authority over both the student halls and the wider context of the Freedom Rides.

During the phone call itself, Ty was positioned centre stage right (CSR), Em and CJ sat on the stools upstage centre (USC), and Dayz in role as Diane Nash was centre stage left (CSL). The stools were set at the back of the space — USR one of the larger stools, then working across to almost centre stage where the two small stools were, with the final taller stool USL.

The three steel flats remained at the back of the space. On the flat USR was the confederate flag, the centre flat held the Ku Klux Klan hat, Uncle George’s cowboy hat, and Bull Connor’s hat. The flat USL had President Kennedy’s red tie and the LWG’s headband — creating a visual reminder of all the characters and the story so far.

Physicality: Diane Nash vs the US Representative

Diane Nash remained stoic and strong, rooted on the spot throughout the conversation. She maintained a straight, strong, tall back and neck with her hands placed elegantly in front of her. This physicality reinforced that she was grounded in her beliefs and would not be moved.

On the line “You elected me as your leader,” Dayz used strong muscle tension to outstretch her right arm with the palm facing up on “you” — referencing the students. On “me,” she quickly placed her palm across her chest in a patriotic fashion, reinforcing that this issue was close to her heart.

Key Fact — Contrasting Physicality

The US representative (played by Ty) contrasted sharply with Diane Nash. He used quick-paced exaggerated movements and a fast pace of speech, showing he was under pressure. Meanwhile, CJ and Em used ensemble movement to quickly turn their heads from side to side depending on which character was speaking — like watching a tennis match — directing the audience’s attention to whoever had the dialogue.

CJ in role as Bobby Kennedy said “who the hell is Diane Nash?” using a loud volume and authoritative tone with a slow, considered pace. He elongated the word “hell,” suggesting to the audience he did not know who she was and was trying to recall the name.

Dayz as Diane Nash used a loud and authoritative tone when addressing the students, signifying she was genuine and determined. On the line “I do not shrink from it” (referring to being jailed for protesting), she used a staccato rhythm with clear pauses between words, slowing the sentence down to reinforce she would not back down.

The US representative said “Young woman, do you not understand? You are going to get somebody killed!” using a loud volume, aggressive tone, and fast pace. This patronising delivery showed he was feeling the pressure of Diane Nash’s refusal to back down.

The most powerful line was: “We signed our wills, we know someone will get killed.” This was delivered in a sombre and serious tone, highlighting to the audience the extremely serious nature of the protests and the grave danger the Freedom Riders placed themselves in. This line should have a huge impact on audience members, making them question how far they would go for what they believe in.

Lighting: A white lighting wash was used at the start when Ty answered the phone. When the location changed to Bobby Kennedy’s office, the wash was removed and a white Fresnel spotlight was placed on Bobby Kennedy and the US representative. CJ and Em could not be seen. A white wash with a blue tinge was then used to show the change of location — the blue highlighted that the Black community felt isolated. The white wash returned for the phone call so all actors were visible.

Sound: A snapshot of the American national anthem was used to open the scene, highlighting that CJ was taking on the role of Bobby Kennedy. A staccato rhythm with a deep, threatening tone signalled the change of location to Diane Nash’s flashback. Slow-paced, emotive, sombre music played at a low level when Diane Nash addressed the students, adding to the emotional atmosphere. Another snapshot of the anthem after “It is up to you” showed the shift back to Bobby Kennedy’s office.

Key Moment Four: CJ ‘Reminder’ Scene

This scene occurs at approximately 9 minutes into the performance, during the “Hank scene” where the audience meets Thora, Merna, Jim, and other Freedom Riders. The actor CJ asks “like what?” out of role, and Ty breaks from his role as Jim (a White man who joined the Freedom Riders) and says “you can’t have forgotten already? Ok…go for it.”

The Diamond Formation

At the start of the moment, the actors were positioned in a diamond shape:

  • Ty (as Jim) — USL, standing on a small stool at the highest level, reflecting the power status of White people in 1960s society
  • Em (as Thora) — USC
  • Dayz (as Merna) — CS
  • CJ (as Hank) — DSR, at the lowest point

Having Jim (White) on the highest level and Hank (Black) at the lowest, with large proxemics between them, highlighted the large disparity in power and the inequality of the society.

Key Fact — CJ Steps Forward

When CJ asked the question (breaking from character), he took a step forward, putting himself on the same level as Em and Dayz. This simple movement showed that today’s society believes all people should be treated equally regardless of skin colour. Ty then stepped down from his stool to join the female actors — and all three quickly circled CJ, forcing him USC and almost pinning him against the steel flat.

Physicality: The Circling Technique

CJ used closed physicality — closed body language and a hunched posture. He held his hands in front of his chest as if to create a barrier from the other actors circling him. This effectively portrayed how intimidated his character felt. When the sound collage reached full volume, CJ covered his face with both palms to “hide” from the experience, highlighting his character’s distress.

Dayz said “You were told to shut up…” so aggressively that her whole physicality jerked as she shouted. Despite having her back to the audience, the venom in her voice was reflected by jarring movements in her body. She stepped forward, reducing proxemics to CJ, pushed her hands forward in an aggressive gesture, and used a peacocking motion with her head to further intimidate him. She maintained strong muscle tension throughout.

“Like what?” and “I’ve got a lot to remember! What is is?” were spoken by CJ using a cocky tone and slow pace. This showed his character did not understand the significance of his question and was nonchalant about the issues the Freedom Riders faced — highlighting his ignorance.

All three Black actors used a loud volume and aggressive tone when shouting at CJ, creating tension and building an uneasy mood that helped the audience understand how the Freedom Riders would have felt. When CJ could not cope, he shouted “shhh, shh, shut up, shut up, stop, stop, stop! Harsh man” — the loud volume, panicked tone, and quick pace showed he now understood the intimidation and fear.

Immediately after, Ty said “well that’s how they did it” in a calm, matter-of-fact tone at a quieter volume. This shift highlighted to the audience that Ty was satisfied CJ had learnt his lesson and understood the terror the Freedom Riders experienced.

Key Fact — The Aftermath

When CJ begged them to stop, all characters relaxed their posture, loosened their muscle tension, and returned to their “usual” relaxed physicality as the British actors. This clear shift showed the ordeal was over and the rehearsal would continue. CJ physically slumped over at the end — a clear sign to the audience that the experience had taken a physically and emotionally exhausting toll, reinforcing the plight of Black people in 1960s society.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing the Diane Nash and CJ Reminder scenes, always identify the contrast between characters. Strong answers compare two performers’ techniques side by side. For example: “Diane Nash remained stoic with strong posture, whereas the US representative used quick, exaggerated movements. This contrast highlighted Nash’s unshakeable conviction versus the representative’s growing desperation.” Showing you can identify contrasts demonstrates sophisticated understanding of performance skills.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Diane Nash scene uses contrasting physicality (stoic vs frantic) and authoritative voice to show courage and resistance, with lighting changes marking shifts between locations.
  • The CJ Reminder scene uses a diamond formation with levels reflecting power status, a circling technique to build intimidation, and a sound collage to create climax.
  • Both scenes demonstrate how actors can communicate complex themes of inequality, intimidation, and courage through carefully chosen voice and physicality techniques without any set or costume changes.

lessons.title: Design & Performance Evaluation
lessons.description: Costume, set, lighting, sound, and props — how to structure a Section B evaluation essay using SEAS paragraphs.
lessons.content_html:
Costume Design in Rise Up

The costume design in Rise Up was deliberately minimalistic. All four actors wore base costumes only throughout the performance, with no full costume changes at any point. This simplicity was a deliberate design choice that allowed the actors to change roles quickly and kept the performance flowing at a fast pace.

Each actor’s costume communicated something about their character:

  • Em — wore all black: a male-style shirt, black leggings, and black boots. This reflected the society being explored in the play where women were treated as “underdogs.” By wearing a male-style outfit, it showed she still had to take on male characteristics to be seen as successful.
  • Ty — wore all black: formal shirt, trousers, and shoes. This demonstrated his respect for the Freedom Riders — he wore his best clothes to honour their story.
  • Dayz — wore a black and white floral knee-length dress. This reinforced her femininity and showed that you can be successful as a woman. The black and white colours were symbolic: they showed the two races striving for equality and that attitudes to racism are simply “black and white” — right or wrong.
  • CJ — wore black skinny jeans and a black polo shirt. This contrasted with Ty’s formal costume, implying CJ did not think the Freedom Riders were worth dressing up for, showing a lack of initial respect.
Key Fact — White Gloves as Costume Detail

The most significant costume addition was the white gloves worn by Em and Dayz when playing the White shopper characters. Each wore a single glove on opposite hands (Dayz left, Em right), reinforcing they were “as one” and their racist thinking was aligned. For the exam, you could suggest a development: CJ could tuck his shirt in when he realises the truth about racism, or Em could wear red lipstick to symbolise her power.

Key Fact — Remember the Thumbs Rule

When writing about design or performance in Section B, every paragraph must include: Thumbs up (what was successful and why), Thumb towards yourself (impact on you or the audience), and Thumbs down (a development and why it would be more effective). Use this structure for every point you make about costume, set, lighting, sound, or acting.

Set Design

The set was minimal but highly effective. No specific area of the stage was used for a particular location — this was effective because it showed that everyone was accountable for their actions regardless of where they were.

Three steel flats were positioned at the back of the space. These were effective because:

  • The silver surface allowed the audience to reflect on their own behaviour — the reflective material was symbolic
  • They were made to look like a Greyhound bus, with designs on the side and rivet holes for windows
  • They allowed the actors to map the journey of the Freedom Riders in red chalk, showing the dangerous route
  • At the end of the performance, they were turned around to reveal real images of real Freedom Riders — the black and white photographs symbolised that there is only right and wrong when it comes to racism
  • The images were yellowed to show the events happened a long time ago

Four versatile stools were used throughout — two small and two tall:

  • The different heights clearly showed power — Uncle George stood on the tall stool when the Freedom Riders sat on small stools to show they were powerless
  • They were silver to imply they were taken from a diner where racism was prevalent, connecting to the sit-in protests
  • They were turned upside down to create a prison — the legs suggesting prison bars
  • They served as bus seats when the Freedom Riders gripped their sides during the explosion scene

Props

A large number of props were used in Rise Up. Many helped create believable and easily recognisable characters, showing that it was the people who use these objects who made the decision to be racist.

Key props included:

  • Red chalk — used to track the Freedom Riders’ journey on the steel flats. The red colour symbolised the danger and potential for death, as well as the passion the characters felt about equality. The markings resembled a heartbeat monitor, showing the Freedom Riders could lose their lives at any moment.
  • Confederate flag and baseball cap — worn by Southern States characters, reminding the audience of the racist attitudes in the South
  • Cowboy hat (Uncle George) — reminded the audience he was from the Southern States
  • Cigar (Governor Patterson) — symbolised he was an offensive character who did not care for those around him
  • White hat (Bull Connor) — showed he was a Southern man but more educated than a cowboy
  • Ku Klux Klan hood — a powerful reminder that the Klan were prevalent during this time
  • Red tie and microphone (President Kennedy) — the red showed control over danger; the microphone showed the President’s voice was heard worldwide
  • Dayz’s notebook (stolen by CJ) — reminded the audience that all the information was factual
  • LWG’s bow — which CJ refused to wear, demonstrating the “play within a play” convention
Key Fact — Symbolic Staging

Uncle George always remained stage left, implying he was not an honest or genuine character. The Little White Girl always remained stage right, reinforcing her kind, questioning nature. This consistent positioning helped the audience quickly identify moral alignment.

Lighting Design

The lighting in Rise Up was relatively simplistic because it was performed by a touring theatre company. It remained mostly a white lighting wash throughout, with the intention that actors should be visible at all times.

Different lighting states were used for different key moments:

  • Bus explosion — orange shaft of light increasing in intensity, white wash fading, creating shadows that suggested a crowd of Freedom Riders
  • Connor Bull scene — lights at low intensity, lit from above with steel lighting creating shadows and atmosphere
  • Final scenes — lit from all directions at high intensity, white light symbolising honesty and hope
  • White Shoppers — white and blue wash, with intensity increasing when the LWG was introduced to symbolise innocence
  • Prison — lit from behind at low intensity, tight spotlight reminding the audience of imprisonment

Possible developments you could suggest in an exam:

  • A gobo with a leaf pattern when Connor Bull abandoned the Freedom Riders, to show the forest location
  • A slow red strobe when Connor Bull drops the Freedom Riders to symbolise danger and a police car
  • A straw wash changing to intense red during the bus explosion, with pulsating orange and red to create the illusion of flames and symbolise the Freedom Riders’ heartbeats
  • A cold blue wash on the White shoppers with a white spotlight on the LWG, to further isolate her innocence from their racism

Sound Design

Sound was used effectively throughout Rise Up. Key examples included:

  • “Hit the Road Jack” by Ray Charles (1961) — historically accurate to the period, reinforcing the cultural context of the Freedom Rides
  • Bus explosion sounds — banging on the side of the bus, crowd noise building, and a small explosion sound, all creating diegetic atmosphere
  • American national anthem — snippets used to signal Bobby Kennedy scenes and location changes
  • Sound collage — multiple voices layered to build tension and create climax (used in the CJ reminder scene and the bus explosion)
  • Children’s voices — sharing opinions about racism to conclude the performance, bringing the message into the present day

Structuring Your Section B Essay

Use the SEAS paragraph structure for every paragraph in your response:

  • S — State what you observed: “In the bus explosion scene, the lighting changed from a white wash to a small orange shaft of light on the middle steel flat…”
  • E — Explain why it was effective: “This was effective because it clearly showed the audience the bus was alight without requiring a realistic fire effect, fitting the abstract style…”
  • A — Audience impact: “This made the audience fear for the Freedom Riders’ lives and created empathy through the gradual intensity increase…”
  • S — Suggest a development: “This could have been developed by adding a pulsating red and orange strobe to create the illusion of flames…”
Key Fact — Key Evaluation Phrases

Build these into your writing: “This was effective because…”, “In my opinion I thought…”, “However, in reflection…”, “I particularly enjoyed…”, and “I feel that this could have been developed because…” Remember — 10 of your 30 marks come from using drama terminology, so use terms like proxemics, levels, intensity, wash, gobo, and muscle tension in every paragraph.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For design-focused questions, always link the design choice back to meaning. Don’t just describe what you saw — explain what it communicated to the audience. For example, don’t write “the stools were different heights.” Instead write: “The stools were of different heights; this was effective because it clearly showed power. Uncle George stood on a tall stool when the Freedom Riders were sat on small stools, symbolising their powerlessness against the racism of the mob.” Always suggest a development to access the highest marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Costume was minimalistic (base costumes only), with the white gloves being the most significant addition — symbolising the “unified” racist thinking of the White shoppers.
  • Set relied on three steel flats (doubling as a Greyhound bus) and four stools of different heights showing power. The flats were turned at the end to reveal real photographs of the Freedom Riders.
  • Use the SEAS structure (State, Explain, Audience, Suggest) and always link design choices to the communication of meaning — 10 marks are specifically for drama terminology.
